14 This matter came before the Honorable Alberto E. Tolentino on April 23, 2026, for a

16

22

After his arraignment, the Defendant received a total of six ( 6) violations for violating the
following condition of his pre-trial release:
2

alcoholic beverages and/or illegal controlled substances. Defendant shall submit to
4

to testing will be considered a violation. Probation or the Police authorized to search
5
Defendant's residence, vehicle, or person for alcoholic beverages and/or illegal
6 controlled substances. Defendant shall not enter any alcohol establishment. 7

8

9
the court did not impose additional conditions. Plea Agreement (May 31, 2017). Instead, the court
10
11 ordered that "[t]he conditions of release and probation currently imposed upon defendant in
12 connection with CF-0507-14 shall remain in place." Id.

Plea Agreement at 5-6 (Nov. 18, 2015). Prior to the Defendant's fourteenth violation, the People
2
.
3 filed its Motion to Revoke the Defendant's Probation and Impose Jail Sentence ("Motion to
4
Revoke"). Shortly after the Defendant's last warrant was returned approximately seven (7)
5
months later, the Public Defender Service Corporation ("PDSC") was appointed as counsel for
6
the Defendant. Although PDSC filed a Response to the Motion to Revoke, the court granted its
7
Motion to Withdraw due to a conflict ofinterest. The Alternate Public Defender was subsequently
8
9 appointed as the Defendant's counsel.
10
The Defendant then filed his Opposition to the Motion to Revoke, and the court scheduled
11
a Revocation Hearing for both of the Defendant's cases. At the Revocation Hearing, the court
12
heard testimony from Probation regarding his history under their supervision for both matters.
13
14 After hearing the parties' arguments, the court took the matter under advisement.
15 DISCUSSION
16
If the court finds that a defendant has "inexcusably failed to comply with a substantial
17
requirement imposed as a condition of the order," it may revoke probation and sentence or
18
resentence the offender. 9 GCA § 80.66(a)(2). If a court chooses to revoke probation, the court
19
20 may sentence the defendant to any sentence that it may have originally imposed. 9 GCA §
21
80.66(b ). However, it shall not revoke probation for a defendant's violation of a condition unless
22
the court determines that revocation "will best satisfy the ends of justice and the best interests of
23
the public" under all circumstances. 9 GCA § 80.66(a)(2).
24
The Supreme Court of Guam held that "probation is a favor granted by the state, not a
25
26 right to which a criminal defendant is entitled." People v. Camacho, 2009 Guam 6 "if 26 (quoting
27
28
12 See 12th Violation Report (Jan. 29, 2025).

Parkerv. State, 676 N.E.2d 1083, 1085 (Ind. Ct. App. 1997)). To revoke a defendant's probation,
the court must make two determinations. First, the court must "make a factual determination that
2
,r
3 a violation of a condition of probation has actually occurred." Camacho, 2009 Guam 6 27
4
(quoting Parker, 676 N.E.2d 1083 at 1085). If the violation is proven, then the court must
5
"determine if the violation warrants revocation of probation." Id.
6
A. Defendant Root violated the conditions of his probation.
7
The standard for determining whether a probationer violated a condition of probation is
8
9 that "the evidence and the facts be such as reasonably necessary to satisfy the judge that the
10
probationer's conduct has not been as required by the conditions of probation." Camacho, 2009
11
,r ,r
Guam 6 30 (quoting People v. Angoco, 1998 Guam 10 7). When facing revocation, "the
12
defendant bears the burden of showing an excuse for failure to comply with the condition." Id.
13
14 (quoting State v. Peters, 609 A.2d 40, 43 (N.J. 1992)). During Probation's supervision of the
15
Defendant in CF0507-14, he accumulated two (2) violations on pre-trial release and fourteen (14)
16
after the court entered his guilty plea. For CF0109-16, the Defendant received six (6) violations
17
on pre-trial release and three (3) after the court entered his guilty plea.
18
The court can factually determine that all these violations actually occurred after reviewing
19
20 the court's record of events. For instance, his several failures to report to Probation or appear at a
21 court-ordered hearing are supported by four (4 ) bench warrants issued for both cases.13 Notably,
22
the longest period between a court-issued bench warrant and the return of warrant was
23
approximately five (5) years and five (5) months. See Bench Warrant (Oct. 26, 2018); see also
24
25 Return of Warrant (Mar. 29, 2024). The court can factually determine that the Defendant failed to
26
27
13 See Bench Warrant (Apr. 3, 2017); see also Return of Warrant (May 10, 2017); see also Bench Warrant (May 18,
28 2018); see also Return of Warrant (May 21, 2018); see also Bench Warrant (Oct. 26, 2018); see also Return of
Warrant (Mar. 29, 2024); see also Bench Warrant (May 7, 2025); see also Return of Warrant (Dec. 4, 2025).

refrain from ingesting or consuming illegal controlled substances based on his admissions through
declarations, admissions without further testing, or off-island confirmation after challenging his
2
3 test results.14
4
As seen in the court's review of his violations above, the Defendant himself either justified
5
his violations in open court or admitted to them through his written declaration. Based on the
6
violation reports, Probation's testimony at the Revocation Hearing, and the parties' arguments,
7
the court finds that the Defendant has violated multiple conditions of his probation on several
8
9 occas10ns.
10
B. Defendant Root's violations warrant revocation of probation.
11
With regard to probation revocation, the Supreme Court of the United States has noted
12
that "the State clearly has an interest in punishment and deterrence, but this interest can often be
13
14 served fully by alternative means ... [T]he state is not powerless to enforce judgments against
15
those financially unable to pay a fine. For example, the sentencing court could extend the time for
16
making payments, or reduce the fine, or direct that the probationer perform some form of labor or
17
public service in lieu of the fine." Bearden v. Georgia, 461 U.S. 660, 671-72 (internal citations
18
and quotations omitted).
19
20 As mentioned earlier, the court may revoke probation if it finds that the probationer has
21
"inexcusably failed to comply with a substantial requirement imposed as a condition of the order."
22
9 GCA § 80.66(a)(2). In other words, a probationer's violation of probation warrants revoca,tion
23
when the violation upsets the intent of the probation conditions. In Camacho, the Supreme Court
24
25 of Guam held that the probationer's failure to report for drug testing was serious enough to warrant
26
14 For CF0507-14: See Violation Report (Feb. 11. 2016); see also 3rd Violation Report (Mar. 24, 2016); see also 5th
27 Violation Report (Feb. I 0, 2017); see also 6th Violation Report (Feb. 16, 2017); see also 7th Violation Report (Mar.
21, 2017); see also 8th Violation Report (May II, 2017); see also 10th Violation Report (May 18, 2018); see also

For CF0109-16: See 12th Violation Report (Jan. 29, 2025).

revocation when considering the condition being violated was treatment. Camacho, 2009 Guam
,r
6 32. Despite not paying the fine as required under probation, the Supreme Court of Guam
2
3 reasoned that failure to pay a fine alone was not as serious as not reporting for drug tests, because
4
the defendant was convicted of drug-related offenses and had drug testing listed as a condition of
5
probation to ensure the defendant remained sober. Id.
6
Unlike the probationer in Camacho, the Defendant's pending conditions include treatment
7
with Guam Behavioral Health and Wellness Center, fines and court costs, and community service
8
9 hours. During the Revocation Hearing, the People argued that revocation is appropriate in both
lO
cases after ten ( I 0) years of the Defendant's noncompliance with conditions in both his cases. See
11
Revocation Hr'g Mins. at 2:21:04-22:42PM (Apr. 23, 2026).
12
Despite the length of both cases in this court, the Defendant noted that he picked up no
13
14 new cases between 2016 and 2026. See Revocation Hr'g Mins. at 2:22:43 - 30:36PM (Apr. 23,
15 2026). After being in jail for five (5) months, his longest amount of time in jail, the Defendant
16
seeks one last chance to participate in outpatient treatment with Lighthouse Recovery Center
17
(LRC), which he has already signed up to be assessed for. Id.
18
The substantial requirement imposed as a condition in this case was the Defendant's
19
20 completion of treatment. When imposing treatment as a probationary condition, the purpose of
21
doing so is to achieve sustained sobriety for a defendant. In this case, the court gave the Defendant
22
multiple opportunities to complete treatment before considering revocation, such as releasing the
23
Defendant from confinement. For example, the court released the Defendant from confinement
24
after absconding from the court's supervision between 2018 and 2024. Rather than engage in
25
26 treatment services, the Defendant received three (3) more violations and another bench warrant
27
for his arrest, which was returned seven (7) months later.
28
Decision & Order Re. People's Motion to Revoke Defendant's Probation and Impose Jail Sentence

Page 8 of lO

Unless the court determines that revocation "will best satisfy the ends of justice and the
best interests of the public" under all circumstances, the court shall not revoke probation for
2
3 violating a probationary condition. 9 GCA § 80.66(a)(2). Here, the Defendant argues that sending
4
him back to the Department of Corrections ("DOC") would not best satisfy the ends of justice at
5
this time. Rather than revoke his probation, the Defendant seeks at least five (5) months to
6
participate and graduate from a treatment program. See Revocation Hr' g Mins. at 2:22:43 -
7
8 30:36PM.
9 While the Defendant desires to complete treatment outside of DOC with the help of his
IO
family, the Defendant's pattern of release followed by a warrant concerns the court of his ability
11
to complete treatment after being ordered to do so for the past ten years. In Guam, DOC provides
12
a Residential Substance Abuse Treatment ("RSAT") program for its inmates who are battling
13
14 addiction. Rather than leave the Defendant to seek treatment on his own, the court believes that it
15
is in the best interests of the public and will best satisfy the ends of justice for DOC to assist the
16
Defendant on his path to recovery through the RSAT program.
17
Because the Defendant has inexcusably failed to comply with treatment as a substantial
18
condition of his probation, the court finds that revocation of the Defendant's probation will best
19
20 satisfy the ends of justice and the best interests of the public. Therefore, the court grants the
21
People's Motion to Revoke the Defendant's Probation and Impose Jail Sentence.
